whatsHappening.background: Yemen’s crisis is rooted in long-standing tensions between North and South Yemen, but the current war escalated after the Houthi movement seized Sana’a in 2014 and a Saudi-led intervention began in 2015. By late 2025 and early 2026, southern Yemen saw another major power struggle when the UAE-supported Southern Transitional Council advanced in the east, Saudi-backed forces counterattacked, and fears of partition and renewed proxy conflict deepened.

parties.name: Presidential Leadership Council
parties.description: The internationally recognized governing body led by Rashad al-Alimi, which responded politically and militarily to the southern crisis.

parties.name: National Shield Forces
parties.description: Saudi-backed pro-unity forces formed in 2023 that retook territory from STC-aligned forces in early January 2026.

parties.name: Southern Transitional Council
parties.description: A UAE-backed southern secessionist body that seized Hadramawt and al-Mahra in late 2025 before its control collapsed in January 2026.

parties.name: Houthis
parties.description: Armed movement controlling much of northern Yemen and viewing both Saudi Arabia and the UAE as occupiers.

parties.name: AQAP
parties.description: Al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula, which has exploited instability to regain territory and loot arms depots.

timeline.description: North and South Yemen formally merged into the Republic of Yemen, but regional tensions persisted.
The Houthis seized Sana’a and a Saudi-led intervention began in support of the internationally recognized government.
The STC seized Hadramawt and al-Mahra, raising fears of southern secession and renewed proxy conflict.
Saudi-backed National Shield Forces retook territory, STC control collapsed, and Saudi Arabia announced the secessionist body was dissolved.

civilianImpact.experiences: Civilians in Yemen are living through one of the world’s most severe humanitarian crises. More than half the population needs assistance, while aid delivery has been scaled back by a major funding gap. Families face insecurity, economic collapse, human rights abuses, restrictions on movement, and growing danger as armed groups exploit local instability. Women in Houthi-controlled areas face especially harsh limits on travel, work, and aid access.

image.alt: Yemeni civilians affected by the crisis

howToHelp.summary: Yemen’s crisis continues to be shaped by war, underfunding, and fragmented political control. Supporting humanitarian aid and ceasefire efforts can help families facing hunger, displacement, and unsafe living conditions while reducing the risk of deeper proxy conflict.

whatsHappening.background: Yemen’s war affects civilians through hunger, insecurity, rights abuses, and shrinking access to aid. Instability in the south and continued Houthi control in the north have deepened everyday hardship for families already living through years of conflict and economic collapse.

civilianImpact.experiences: Yemenis are not only threatened by direct fighting but also by the collapse of normal life. Armed groups have exploited withdrawn forces and unstable territory, especially in the south. Shipping attacks and retaliatory strikes have harmed ports, livelihoods, and local environments. At the same time, underfunded aid operations leave millions with less food, less protection, and fewer essential services than they need to survive.

howToHelp.summary: Civilians continue to pay the price for conflict, aid shortfalls, and political fragmentation. Humanitarian assistance, protection efforts, and a durable ceasefire remain critical for reducing harm and preventing even deeper instability.

learnMore.text: The crisis affects civil liberties, gender equity, aid access, safety, and long-term local livelihoods.

whatsHappening.background: Support is most effective when it strengthens humanitarian operations already serving families in Yemen and when it backs efforts toward a lasting ceasefire and political settlement. Aid remains essential because millions of civilians are living through hunger, insecurity, displacement, and reduced services while funding continues to fall short.

civilianImpact.experiences: Helping Yemen means supporting both immediate humanitarian relief and longer-term efforts to reduce violence. Donations can help keep food and essential aid moving to vulnerable communities, while public attention and advocacy can strengthen calls for ceasefire, diplomacy, and protection of civilians.

howToHelp.summary: Support humanitarian groups such as the World Food Programme and follow verified updates on Yemen. You can also advocate for diplomacy, civilian protection, and serious international attention to a crisis that remains underfunded despite the scale of need.

learnMore.text: You can also follow UN mediation efforts and humanitarian updates to better understand Yemen’s crisis and support informed advocacy.
